title: Why is the Equal Rights Amendment still not ratified?
summary: Josh and Chuck explain why the Equal Rights Amendment (ERA) remains unratified. They open with a listener correction about the words "suffragette" and "suffragist," then trace the ERA from Alice Paul's 1923 draft (named for Lucretia Mott) through the abolitionist-era fight over the Fourteenth Amendment, congressional opposition led by Emanuel Celler, Eleanor Roosevelt's stance, and Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique fueling the 1970s second wave. Congress passed the ERA in 1972 with a seven-year ratification deadline. Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign helped stall it, and it stalled at 35 states before Nevada, Illinois, and Virginia ratified it, bringing the total to 38 amid disputes over rescissions, the expired deadline, and lawsuits over whether it is now part of the Constitution. They discuss Ruth Bader Ginsburg's push to restart the process, existing federal protections (Civil Rights Act, Equal Pay Act, Violence Against Women Act, Title IX), strict scrutiny for protected classes, the abortion debate, and international comparisons. The episode ends with listener mail about a ninja encounter on a camping trip.

segments.title: Opening banter and listener correction
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter and a listener correction about the terms suffragette (disparaging) versus suffragist, noted by listener Mary Malan Oscars.

segments.title: Origins of the ERA and early drafts
segments.summary: Introduction of the ERA as a proposed amendment guaranteeing equal protection regardless of sex. Alice Paul and Crystal Eastman drafted early versions after the Nineteenth Amendment; Paul named it for Lucretia Mott. The poll finding that many people think equal protection already exists in the Constitution is mentioned.

segments.title: Abolition, the Fourteenth Amendment, and early congressional failure
segments.summary: Women's rights advocates asked to add sex to the Fourteenth Amendment, which did not happen, leaving suffragists disappointed. The 1923 version was reworded, and it was introduced in nearly every Congress for about fifty years without passing, with few women in Congress.

segments.title: Eleanor Roosevelt, Emanuel Celler, and shifting party positions
segments.summary: Emanuel Celler blocked the ERA from a vote in the House Judiciary Committee. Eleanor Roosevelt opposed it over workplace protections, later softening, and debated Alice Paul. Elizabeth Holtzman defeated Celler in 1972 largely over his ERA opposition.

segments.title: Second wave feminism and The Feminine Mystique
segments.summary: Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique, arising from a college reunion survey, sold a million copies and helped launch second-wave feminism. Mrs. America's depiction of Friedan is mentioned.

segments.title: Congressional passage in 1972, ratification and the seven-year deadline
segments.summary: Congress passed the ERA in 1972 with large majorities. Ratification needed 38 states, and the deadline of seven years was attached to the legislation, not the amendment text. Initially 30 states ratified within a year.

segments.title: Phyllis Schlafly and the STOP ERA campaign
segments.summary: Phyllis Schlafly's STOP ERA campaign argued the amendment would remove women's protections and ruin the family, linking the ERA with abortion, gay rights, and other culture-war issues. Hosts describe her debates with Betty Friedan and her political background, and say the campaign halted ratification at 35 states.

segments.title: Ratification revival, rescissions, and the 38th state
segments.summary: Nevada, Illinois, and Virginia ratified in the 2017 to 2020 period, reaching 38 states, though five states had rescinded earlier ratifications and the deadline had passed. Lawsuits followed over whether the amendment is now part of the Constitution, and Ruth Bader Ginsburg argued for starting over.

segments.title: Existing federal protections and protected classes
segments.summary: The hosts review existing laws (Civil Rights Act, Equal Pay Act, Violence Against Women Act, Title IX) and case law. Ginsburg's Fourteenth Amendment arguments made sex a protected class, and strict scrutiny is explained. Scalia's view that the Constitution does not protect against sex discrimination is cited.

segments.title: Listener mail: ninja in Connecticut
segments.summary: Listener Drew Carroll describes a camping trip in Connecticut where a ninja demonstrated a one-inch punch on him, sending him into a tent stake. The hosts tease the listener mail contest.
